The size of High Peak's population remained relatively unchanged between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

Population size remained stable

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of High Peak remained at 90,900.

In 2021, High Peak was home to around 1.2 people per football pitch-sized piece of land. This area was among the lowest 20% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

The size of High Peak's population didn't change between the last two censuses

An older High Peak

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of High Peak increased by three years, from 43 to 46 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the East Midlands as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by around 2,500 (an increase of 28.4%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 4,200 (20.5% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 2.7 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Fewer couples with dependent children

High Peak saw the East Midlands' largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of households including a couple with dependent children (from 20.5% in 2011 to 17.8% in 2021).

Derbyshire Dales saw the East Midlands' next largest decrease in the percentage of households including a couple with dependent children (from 19.2% in 2011 to 16.6% in 2021).

Across the East Midlands, the percentage of households including a couple with dependent children fell from 19.7% to 18.8%, while the percentage in nearby the Derbyshire Dales fell from 19.2% to 16.6%.

The percentage of households including a couple with dependent children in High Peak decreased by 2.7 percentage points

High Peak residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 85,100 High Peak residents said they were born in England. This represented 93.6% of the local population. The figure has decreased from just under 85,500 in 2011, which at the time represented 94.0% of High Peak's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with around 1,000 High Peak residents reporting this country of birth (1.1%). This figure was down from just over 1,100 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.3% of the population of High Peak.

The number of High Peak residents born in Wales fell from just under 750 in 2011 (0.8% of the local population) to around 700 in 2021 (0.8%).

In 2021, 93.6% of High Peak residents reported their country of birth as England

Unpaid care in High Peak

High Peak saw the East Midlands' joint third-largest percentage-point fall (alongside Rutland) in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 8.0% in 2011 to 4.8% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Across the region, only Derbyshire Dales (from 9.0% to 5.3%) and North East Derbyshire (from 8.5% to 5.2%) saw a greater decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care.

Every local authority area across the East Midlands saw a fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care, as the regional proportion fell from 7.4% to 4.6%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in High Peak decreased by 3.2 percentage points

Religion in High Peak

In 2021, 44.4% of High Peak residents reported having "No religion", up from 27.6% in 2011. The rise of 16.8 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in High Peak. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the East Midlands, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.5% to 40.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 48.5% of people in High Peak described themselves as Christian (down from 64.1%), while 5.7% did not state their religion (down from 7.2% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Read the bulletin Religion, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 44.4% of usual residents in High Peak reported having "No religion"

Fall in employment

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in nearby the Derbyshire Dales (4.5 percentage points) than in High Peak (1.9 percentage points).

In High Peak, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) decreased from 59.7% in 2011 to 57.8% in 2021. During the same period, the percentage in nearby the Derbyshire Dales decreased from 57.9% to 53.4%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in High Peak fell from 3.5% to 2.2%, while the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were retired (economically inactive) increased from 23.0% to 26.1%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in High Peak decreased by 1.9 percentage points

Change in work hours

In 2021, 10.5% of High Peak residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure increased from 10.0% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in nine people (10.9%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 13.4% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 56.4% to 57.8%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week remained 9.8% across the East Midlands. Across England, the percentage increased from 9.7% to 10.3%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in High Peak increased by 0.5 percentage points

Health in High Peak

In 2021, 49.2% of High Peak residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 46.9% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.1% to 33.6%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of High Peak residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.0% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 4.2% to 3.6%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very bad health in High Peak decreased by 0.2 percentage points

Ethnic groups in High Peak

In 2021, 1.3% of High Peak residents identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category, up from 1.0% in 2011. The 0.3 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the East Midlands, the percentage of people from "Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups" increased from 1.9% to 2.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 2.3% to 3.0%.

In 2021, 97.4% of people in High Peak identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 97.9% in 2011), while 0.8% identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category (also 0.8% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.1% in 2011 to 0.2% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.

Read the bulletin Ethnic group, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 1.3% of usual residents in High Peak identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category

National identity in High Peak

In 2021, 2.9% of High Peak residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 2.0% in 2011.

In 2021, 1.2% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.4% in 2011. The percentage of residents in High Peak that identified as "British only" increased from 15.3% to 58.3%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the East Midlands (2.7 percentage points, from 5.8% to 8.5%) than in High Peak (0.9 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in High Peak increased by 0.9 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of High Peak residents aged 16 years and over, 33.6% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 30.9% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in two people (46.8%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 49.4% in 2011. The percentage of adults in High Peak that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.9% to 10.6%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater across the East Midlands (3.8 percentage points, from 32.3% to 36.1%) than in High Peak (2.7 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in High Peak increased by 2.7 percentage points

Change in housing in High Peak

Of High Peak households, 71.0% owned their home in 2021, down from 72.0% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in six households (16.1%) rented privately, compared with 13.4% in 2011. The percentage of High Peak households that lived in a socially rented property decreased from 12.7% to 12.2%.

The decrease in the percentage of households that owned their home was greater across the East Midlands (1.8 percentage points, from 67.2% to 65.5%) than in High Peak (1.1 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.0 percentage points, from 63.3% to 61.3%.

The rate of home ownership in High Peak decreased by 1.1 percentage points

Disability in High Peak

In 2021, 7.0% of High Peak residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 8.6% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in High Peak (1.6 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the East Midlands (1.6 percentage points, from 9.3% to 7.7%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in High Peak decreased by 1.6 percentage points
